title: Anatomy of a Delta Table on OneLake
purpose: Show what a Delta table actually is on disk in OneLake — immutable Parquet objects plus a numbered, checkpointed transaction log — and how that log gives ADLS Gen2 object storage ACID semantics through optimistic concurrency and snapshot-isolated reads.
accessibleSummary: An internals diagram: a write stages new immutable Parquet objects, then races to atomically create the next-numbered JSON commit file in the table's _delta_log folder — only one writer can win a given commit number, so a losing writer detects the collision and retries. Every ten commits, the log is folded into a Parquet checkpoint so metadata reads stay fast as history grows. A reader pins to the newest fully-committed log record at query start and reconstructs its snapshot from that checkpoint plus a few trailing commits, so concurrent writers never produce a dirty read. A warning node covers what happens when two writers race for the same commit number.
longDescription: This is an internals diagram of the physical and logical structure of a Delta table stored in OneLake. Physically, a Delta table is two things: a set of immutable Parquet data objects, and a write-ahead transaction log kept in a _delta_log subfolder. The log, not a directory listing, is the single source of truth for which Parquet objects currently belong to the table, which is what gives ADLS Gen2-style object storage ACID table semantics on top of storage that has no native transactions. Each commit is a zero-padded, sequentially numbered JSON file (000003.json, 000004.json, and so on) holding add and remove actions that record which Parquet objects entered or left the table, alongside metaData, protocol, and commitInfo records. Writers achieve serializability through optimistic concurrency rather than locking: a writer stages its new Parquet objects independently of any other writer, then attempts to atomically create the single next-numbered log file. Only one writer can win a given commit number; a losing writer detects the collision, rereads the current table state, and retries its commit at the next number. On ADLS Gen2, that atomicity is implemented through an atomic rename that fails if the target name already exists. As history grows, the log is periodically folded into a Parquet checkpoint (every 10 commits by default) that consolidates still-relevant actions and drops superseded ones, so a reader reconstructs current state from the latest checkpoint plus a handful of trailing JSON commits rather than replaying the entire log from commit zero. Readers achieve snapshot isolation by pinning to the newest fully-committed log record at the moment a query starts, so concurrent writers landing new commits mid-query are never observed — this is also the mechanism behind Delta time travel, since any earlier state can be reconstructed by replaying the log only up to an older commit ID.

nodes.label: Immutable Parquet data objects
nodes.summary: The physical rows of the table, stored as immutable Parquet files.
nodes.detail: A Delta table's actual row data lives as immutable Parquet objects. Files are never edited in place — any change (insert, update, delete) is expressed by writing new Parquet objects and/or recording that existing ones are removed, never by rewriting bytes inside an existing file.
nodes.whyItMatters: Immutability is what makes optimistic concurrency and time travel possible in the first place: because no existing object is ever mutated, two writers can stage new objects independently without racing over shared file contents.

evidence.note: OneLake's Delta-format tables store data as immutable Parquet objects plus a write-ahead transaction log in a _delta_log subfolder; the log, not a directory listing, is the single source of truth for which Parquet objects currently belong to the table.

inputs: Row data from a Spark write, MERGE, or T-SQL DML operation
processing: Rows are serialised into one or more new Parquet objects
Existing objects affected by the write are marked for removal in the upcoming commit, never edited in place
outputs: A set of new Parquet objects, staged in storage but not yet part of the table until the commit lands
drill.example: An UPDATE affecting 200 rows in a 50-file table writes new Parquet objects containing the updated rows' file(s) and marks the original file(s) containing those rows for removal — no existing Parquet file's bytes are ever rewritten.
controls: File size targets (BinSize) that determine how many new objects a write produces
V-Order and compression settings applied at write time
failureModes: Unmanaged small-file accumulation from many small commits, since old objects are never rewritten in place — only compaction consolidates them
Assuming an in-place edit occurred when in fact old and new objects briefly coexist until commit

nodes.label: _delta_log: numbered JSON commits
nodes.summary: Each commit is a zero-padded, sequentially numbered JSON file recording add/remove actions.
nodes.detail: Each commit to a Delta table is a zero-padded, sequentially numbered JSON file in _delta_log (e.g. 000003.json) holding an array of actions: add and remove record which Parquet objects entered or left the table, while metaData and protocol record schema/configuration and commitInfo records operation metadata.
nodes.whyItMatters: The log is the actual source of truth for table membership, not a directory listing — a query engine determines which Parquet files belong to the table by reading the log, not by listing the folder, which is what lets OneLake give ACID semantics on top of plain object storage.

evidence.note: Each commit to a Delta table in OneLake is a zero-padded, sequentially numbered JSON file in _delta_log (e.g. 000003.json) holding an array of actions: add and remove record which Parquet objects entered or left the table, metaData and protocol record schema/configuration.

inputs: Staged new Parquet objects and the set of objects being removed by this write
processing: Assemble the add/remove/metaData/commitInfo actions describing this write
Attempt to write them as the next sequentially numbered JSON file
outputs: A new immutable commit record that, once it lands, becomes the new authoritative table state
drill.example: Commit 000047.json records that Parquet files part-01a.parquet and part-01b.parquet were added while part-00f.parquet was removed, alongside commitInfo noting it was an UPDATE operation.
controls: Commit granularity (one logical operation per commit)
failureModes: Treating a directory listing of the Parquet folder as the table state instead of reading the log — this omits removed-but-not-yet-vacuumed files and orphaned uncommitted objects

nodes.label: Optimistic concurrency: atomic commit race
nodes.summary: Only one writer wins a given commit number; the loser detects the collision and retries.
nodes.detail: OneLake's Delta tables achieve write serializability through optimistic concurrency rather than locking: a writer stages new Parquet objects independently, then atomically creates the single next-numbered log JSON file; only one writer can win that specific commit number. The atomic 'only one writer wins' guarantee is implemented differently per storage backend; on ADLS Gen2 it is implemented via an atomic rename that fails if the target name already exists.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is what lets multiple concurrent writers (e.g. two Spark jobs writing to the same table) stay safe without a lock manager — the losing writer's own retry logic, not a coordinator, resolves the race.

evidence.note: OneLake's Delta tables achieve write serializability through optimistic concurrency rather than locking: a writer stages new Parquet objects independently, then atomically creates the single next-numbered log JSON file; only one writer can win that specific commit number.

The atomic 'only one writer wins this commit number' guarantee is implemented differently per storage backend; on ADLS Gen2 (which OneLake is built on) that atomicity is implemented via an atomic rename that fails if the target name already exists.

inputs: Two or more writers with staged Parquet objects, both attempting to commit against the same current table version
processing: Each writer attempts an atomic create/rename of the same next-numbered log file
Only one create succeeds; the storage layer's atomicity guarantee prevents both from winning
outputs: One winning commit that becomes the new table state; one (or more) losing attempts that must retry
drill.example: Two Spark jobs both try to write commit 000048.json at the same moment; the storage layer's atomic rename lets only one succeed, and the second job's write fails with a conflict, triggering its retry logic.
controls: Retry logic and backoff in the writing engine
failureModes: A writer with no retry logic simply failing on collision instead of rereading state and reattempting — see the warning node
High-concurrency write patterns against one table causing repeated retries and wasted work under contention

nodes.label: Trap: unhandled commit collisions
nodes.summary: A writer that doesn't retry on collision fails outright instead of safely reattempting.
nodes.detail: Because only one writer can win a given commit number, any concurrent writer must reread the current table state and retry its commit at the next number when it loses the race. A client that does not implement this retry behaviour simply fails the write on collision rather than completing it safely.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is a real operational trap for teams writing custom Delta clients or highly concurrent jobs against the same table: without retry logic, perfectly valid concurrent writes fail intermittently under contention instead of completing.

evidence.note: Only one writer can win a specific commit number in OneLake's optimistic concurrency model; a losing writer must reread state and retry rather than assume its write succeeded.

inputs: Two or more writers concurrently targeting the same Delta table
processing: Detect a failed atomic commit as a normal, expected outcome under concurrency, not an error to surface to the user
Reread the latest table version and retry the write at the next commit number
outputs: Both writers eventually succeed (serialised), rather than one failing outright
drill.example: A high-frequency streaming job and a scheduled batch job both write to the same table; without retry handling, the batch job's commit fails outright during a collision window instead of quietly retrying and succeeding moments later.
controls: Using a Delta-aware engine (Spark, the documented Delta connectors) that implements retry natively rather than a hand-rolled writer
failureModes: Intermittent, hard-to-reproduce write failures under concurrent load that look like flaky infrastructure but are actually unhandled commit collisions
High-concurrency write patterns against one table amplifying retry storms if backoff is not implemented

nodes.label: Checkpoint (every 10 commits)
nodes.summary: The log is periodically folded into a Parquet checkpoint so metadata reads stay fast.
nodes.detail: To keep metadata reads fast as a Delta table accumulates history, the underlying Delta engine periodically compacts the log into a Parquet checkpoint (every 10 commits by default) that folds in every still-relevant add/remove/metadata action and drops superseded ones. Checkpoint writing is best-effort and separate from the atomic commit itself, so a client that crashes mid-checkpoint leaves the table's actual data unaffected.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without checkpointing, reconstructing table state on a long-lived table would mean replaying thousands of small JSON commits on every query — the checkpoint is what keeps metadata discovery fast regardless of how much history a table has accumulated.

evidence.note: To keep metadata reads fast as a Delta table accumulates history, OneLake's underlying Delta engine periodically compacts the log into a Parquet checkpoint (every 10 commits by default) that folds in every still-relevant add/remove/metadata action and drops superseded ones.

Checkpoint compaction is safe to skip or fail: since checkpoint writing and the pointer file that records the newest checkpoint ID are both best-effort and separate from the atomic commit itself, a client that crashes mid-checkpoint leaves the table's actual data unaffected.

inputs: The accumulated sequence of JSON commit files since the last checkpoint
processing: Fold every still-relevant add/remove/metadata action into one Parquet checkpoint file
Update the pointer file recording the newest checkpoint ID
outputs: A consolidated Parquet checkpoint that summarises table state as of that commit, replacing the need to replay from commit zero
drill.example: A table at commit 000090 has a checkpoint written at commit 000090 (a multiple of 10); a reader at commit 000094 reads that checkpoint plus commits 91-94, rather than all 94 commits from the start.
failureModes: A crash mid-checkpoint-write, which is safe by design since the commit itself is unaffected, but can leave a stale or missing checkpoint pointer requiring the next checkpoint attempt to catch up
Extremely long gaps without a successful checkpoint (e.g. from repeated failures) slowing metadata reads back down toward full-log replay

nodes.label: Snapshot-isolated read
nodes.summary: A reader pins to the newest fully-committed log record at query start and never sees later writes.
nodes.detail: Delta table readers achieve snapshot isolation by pinning their read to whatever the newest fully-committed log record ID is at the moment they start: they reconstruct table state as of that version and never observe files added or removed by commits that land after the read began. Because every add and remove action in the log stays immutable and versioned, this same mechanism supports time travel — a client can reconstruct any earlier table state by replaying the log only up to an older commit ID.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is what guarantees a long-running query never sees a half-written or inconsistent table, even while other writers are actively committing new data in parallel — and it is the same mechanism that makes time travel and accidental-overwrite recovery possible.

evidence.note: Delta table readers achieve snapshot isolation by pinning their read to whatever the newest fully-committed log record ID is at the moment they start: they reconstruct table state as of that version and never observe files added or removed by commits that land after the read began.

Because every add and remove action in the log stays immutable and versioned, OneLake's Delta tables support time travel: a client can reconstruct any earlier table state by replaying the log only up to an older commit ID, which is also how accidental overwrites can be corrected.

inputs: The latest checkpoint plus trailing commits as of the moment a query starts
processing: Reconstruct the table's file manifest as of the pinned commit version
Read only the Parquet objects present in that reconstructed snapshot
outputs: Query results consistent with a single point-in-time table version, unaffected by concurrent writers
drill.example: A five-minute analytical query starts against commit 000094; three new commits land from a concurrent Spark job while it runs, but the query's results reflect only the state as of 000094, exactly as if no writes had occurred.
controls: Time-travel version/timestamp selection for historical queries
failureModes: Assuming a long-running read reflects writes that landed mid-query — it does not, by design
VACUUM removing Parquet objects still referenced by an old commit a time-travel query needs, if run with too short a retention window

commit attempt races for the next number
risk if the loser has no retry logic
losing writer rereads state and retries
every 10 commits, folded into a checkpoint
readers reconstruct state from checkpoint + trailing commits

walkthrough.title: Start: immutable Parquet data objects
walkthrough.explanation: A Delta table's rows live as immutable Parquet files; writes stage new objects rather than editing existing ones in place.

walkthrough.title: Every write is a numbered log commit
walkthrough.explanation: New Parquet objects only become part of the table once a zero-padded, sequentially numbered JSON commit records them as added — the log, not a directory listing, is the source of truth.

walkthrough.title: Concurrent writers race for the same commit number
walkthrough.explanation: Only one writer can atomically win a given commit number; on OneLake's ADLS Gen2 foundation this is enforced by an atomic rename that fails if the target already exists.

walkthrough.title: Warning: a losing writer must retry, not fail
walkthrough.explanation: A writer without retry logic simply fails the write on collision — a real operational trap for hand-rolled or highly concurrent Delta clients.

walkthrough.title: Feedback: retries loop back into new commits
walkthrough.explanation: A losing writer rereads current state and retries at the next commit number, looping back into the same log — and every 10 commits, that growing log is folded into a Parquet checkpoint to keep metadata reads fast.

walkthrough.title: End: readers get a consistent snapshot
walkthrough.explanation: A reader pins to the newest fully-committed record at query start and reconstructs its view from the checkpoint plus trailing commits, guaranteeing it never sees a half-written table — the same mechanism that powers time travel.
